paper_identity.title: Gut dysbiosis contributes to amyloid pathology, associated with C/EBP beta/AEP signaling activation in Alzheimer's disease mouse model

final_report_expectations.research_question: Whether gut dysbiosis contributes to amyloid pathology in Alzheimer's disease mouse models through activation of C/EBP beta/AEP signaling, and whether antibiotics, R13, or Lactobacillus salivarius modulate this pathway.
final_report_expectations.study_design: Original preclinical mouse study using age-dependent microbiome profiling, 5xFAD and 3xTg AD models, cohousing/dirty-bedding microbiome exposure, chronic antibiotic treatment, R13 treatment, probiotic feeding, brain/gut pathology assays, and behavior tests.
final_report_expectations.population_or_materials: 5xFAD mice, 3xTg mice, wild-type mice, fecal/stool microbiome samples, antibiotic-treated mice, R13-treated mice, live or boiled Lactobacillus salivarius, brain and colon tissues.
methods: 16S rRNA V4 sequencing used Illumina MiSeq with QIIME/UPARSE/Greengenes analysis.
Young 3xTg mice were exposed by cohousing/dirty bedding to aged 3xTg or aged WT mouse microbiota.
R13 dosing and live/boiled L. salivarius probiotic experiments were performed.

Assays included immunoblotting, immunofluorescence/IHC, ELISA, AEP enzymatic assays, FITC-dextran gut permeability, thioflavin S staining, electron microscopy, Golgi staining, Morris water maze, and fear conditioning.
primary_findings: 5xFAD mice developed age-dependent gut dysbiosis associated with activation of C/EBP beta/AEP signaling in gut tissue.
Microbiota from aged 3xTg mice, unlike aged WT microbiota, accelerated brain AD pathology and cognitive dysfunction in young 3xTg mice.
Antibiotic treatment suppressed C/EBP beta/AEP signaling, reduced amyloidogenic processing/pathology, and improved cognitive outcomes in 5xFAD mice.
R13 blunted gut C/EBP beta/AEP signaling and reduced gut amyloid pathology, while R13-associated L. salivarius contributed to reduced gut leakage and oxidative stress.
secondary_findings: Microbiome changes included decreased diversity and shifts in Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, Helicobacter, Prevotella, Sutterella, and related taxa.
R13 reduced Helicobacter hepaticus expansion and increased beneficial taxa including L. salivarius and Bacteroides ovatus.
Live L. salivarius, more than boiled control, suppressed C/EBP beta/AEP signaling and gut leakage but was not sufficient alone to reverse cognitive deficits.
sensitivity_analysis: No formal sensitivity analysis was reported.

Design-level checks included age comparisons, WT versus AD-model comparisons, aged 3xTg versus aged WT microbiota exposure, vehicle versus antibiotic/R13/probiotic treatments, and live versus boiled L. salivarius controls.
Investigators were blinded to group allocation during animal experiments according to methods.
statistical_tests_used: Data were expressed as mean +/- SEM from three or more independent experiments.
Student's t test was used for two-group comparisons.
One-way ANOVA followed by least significant difference post hoc test was used for more than two groups.
interpretation: The paper supports a mouse-model gut-brain-axis mechanism in which dysbiosis activates C/EBP beta/AEP signaling linked to amyloid/Tau pathology.
R13 should be described as a preclinical intervention with multiple proposed mechanisms, not as proven human AD therapy.
limitations: Mouse-model evidence only; human clinical efficacy is not established.
R13 was noted as under phase 1 clinical trial, but this paper's efficacy evidence is preclinical.
The paper acknowledges uncertainty about exactly how gut microbiota alteration mediates brain BDNF levels.
tables_figures_supplements: Figures 1-7 cover microbiome shifts, cohousing effects, gut C/EBP beta/AEP activation, antibiotic treatment, R13 treatment, R13 microbiome effects, and L. salivarius effects.
Supplementary figures S1-S7 are cited for additional microbiome, pathway, antibiotic, R13, and probiotic analyses.
final_report_expectations.supplement_availability: The PDF states supplementary material is available through the Science Advances article page; extracted main-PDF text cites multiple supplementary figures but does not include full supplement content.
uniqueness: Links gut dysbiosis to AD-like amyloid pathology through the C/EBP beta/AEP pathway.
Combines microbiome profiling, microbiota exposure, gut permeability, brain pathology, and behavior.
Separates antibiotic, R13, and probiotic mechanisms within one preclinical gut-brain-axis model.

critical_claims.claim: Gut dysbiosis occurred in 5xFAD mice in an age-dependent manner and was associated with activation of C/EBP beta/AEP signaling.
Aged 3xTg microbiota exposure increased gut leakage, activated brain C/EBP beta/AEP signaling, reduced synapses, and impaired cognition in young 3xTg mice compared with aged WT microbiota exposure.
Chronic antibiotic treatment reduced C/EBP beta/AEP signaling and amyloid/Tau pathology markers and improved behavioral outcomes in 5xFAD mice.
R13 decreased gut C/EBP beta/AEP signaling, gut A beta signals, AEP activity, gut leakage, and IL-6 in 5xFAD mice.
R13 increased L. salivarius, and live L. salivarius reduced C/EBP beta/AEP signaling, gut leakage, and oxidative stress, but probiotic treatment alone did not reverse cognitive deficits.

report_should_not_claim: Do not claim R13, antibiotics, or L. salivarius is clinically proven to treat human Alzheimer's disease.
Do not omit that the evidence is from mouse models and mechanistic assays.
Do not state that probiotic treatment alone reversed cognitive deficits.
scoring_focus: Preserve the C/EBP beta/AEP mechanistic axis.
Differentiate 5xFAD age/dysbiosis, 3xTg cohousing, antibiotic, R13, and L. salivarius experiments.
Reward correct handling of supplement-dependent supporting evidence and preclinical limits.
